CHAPTER 1 – IDENTITY
Food is closely connected with identity, both constructed and perceived –
what you eat, what you choose not to eat, where you eat it, how you eat it, how it
makes you smell, what you know about the things you eat and so on. In this
chapter I will consider what food can say about one’s identity, and look at the
strategies individuals use to construct an image, both inwardly for themselves,
and outwardly in society.
Law (2001) in ‘Home Cooking: Filipino Women and Geographies of the
Senses in Hong Kong’ experiences and explores in detail how Filipino identity is
enacted on Sundays in Hong Kong through multi-sensory channels: not only taste,
but smell, touch by eating with their hands, the sounds of their own language and
dialects and even the physical closeness of being in large groups. However this is
also a very un-self-conscious expression and enactment of their ethic identity
which has faced criticism from other residents of Hong Kong; it marks out
Filipino domestic workers as a distinct group and does not constitute an effective
strategy of integration. One could argue that their social and legal status in Hong
Kong does not allow them to truly integrate into society, however in the broader
context of migration, it is worth noting that flamboyant expressions of ethnic
identity have alienating as well as unifying effects.
In Consuming Geographies (Bell and Valentine, 1997, p. 135), the
relationship between food and cosmopolitan identity is explained, albeit in a
quite general and generic sense. People, presumably most likely middle class, or
tourists as per Bauman (1997), exhibit cosmopolitanism as a sign of cultural and
even economic superiority by knowing about and being comfortable with exotic
cuisines
26
© 2026 steflai.github.io - All Rights Reserved.
These are two contrasting approaches to using food practices to build an
identity for oneself. In the case of Hong Kong Chinese migrants in London, I have
observed elements that resemble the observations in both the above references.
In the current cultural climate in which foreign cuisines are gaining huge
popularity in London; one just has to look at a recent edition of Time Out to see
recommendations for food from many countries; it is also interesting to consider
how migrants’ insider knowledge could be used to a similar effect as explained in
Consuming Geographies (ibid.) to gain cultural capital.
In Distinction, Bourdieu (1997) noted a consistent correlation between
economic and cultural capital and the types of food that people chose to eat, with
marked differences between those with different levels of economic and cultural
capital (2008, p. 186). While Bourdieu was primarily concerned with class in
conducting this study, it also clearly shows that individuals are concerned with
how they are perceived by what foods they choose when their social and
economic statuses change, as well as considerations such as nutrition and health.
In the case of the young migrant from Hong Kong, who in this case has
fairly high economic and cultural capital, the issue of class in a Western sense is
not fully applicable, as discussed in the introduction. However it is useful to
consider the idea that food choices are a result of as well as a reflection on social
and economic capital, especially since migrants’ identity could be a form of social
capital.
Another way in which identity is created is described in the introductory
chapter to Making Race Matter (Alexander and Knowles, 2005, p. 13). In a
discussion about race and individuals’ bodies, bodies are described the focus of
subjectivity, meaning that there is a constant struggle between an individuals’
27
© 2026 steflai.github.io - All Rights Reserved.
internal attempts to create him/herself as a subject, and external and historic
constraints. In a similar way, it is important to remember that identity, both
physical and otherwise, is not just what a person creates and projects, it is also
working with or pushing against social and cultural preconceptions.
This chapter is divided into three sub-sections derived from common
themes in data collected from the field, they will revolve around the questions:
What does food tell us about a person’s identity? And how do individuals use
food to construct an identity, both inwardly and outwardly? What does this tell
us about them and their positioning in society?
1.1 ‘Do you miss Chinese food?’
‘Do you miss Chinese food?’ is often one of the first questions I ask in an
interview as it links together food and emotion, and it also an everyday question
that is a good starting point for talking. The question also links into Seremetakis’
(1994) and Sutton’s (2001) research on Greek foods and the themes of nostalgia
and memory associated with home foods, which I have also used to provide
context for this question at the beginning of interviews.
The question has elicited surprisingly divided responses, with some
participants quite strongly against sentimentality towards food, and others with
quite willing to admit an emotional element to their liking and occasional craving
for Chinese food.
Amongst the negative responses, practicality was a strong push-back
against what seemed to be seen as a level of sentimentality that participants
seemed to think was quite distinctly ‘Western’, especially as the Chinese tend to
be more reserved and also take pride in it. Ernest in particular was dismissive of
28
© 2026 steflai.github.io - All Rights Reserved.
emotional responses. ‘The Chinese are very practical.’ he said, ‘It is not about the
heart… and it is so easy and convenient to get Chinese food in London,’ he said,
‘there is no need to miss it.’
Claire’s response added another dimension to the rejection of and overtly
emotional response to home foods: ‘I think that [recreating foods at home] is
something that fist generation immigrants do a lot. Like my parents in Norway,
the migrants will make every thing themselves, because if they want dim sum or
something they have to go to Oslo. They can even make 腸粉 (coeng fan, steamed
rice sheet rolls). But in London we have so much choice if we want Chinese.’
She draws a sharp distinction between the older or first generation
Chinese migrants and her own generation. Convenience and availability is the
reason given for not having to make Chinese food at home, however it is quite
easy to imagine that if her parents and their friends were in London, they would
probably still prefer to make some foods themselves due to the real or perceived
quality and variety of foods available.
So far three characteristics that would go towards defining a migrant
identity have come up. The push back against overt sentimentality as something
that is ‘Western’ seeks to keep Chinese-ness separate, while practicality is raised
as a strong point of being Chinese. The separation from first generation migrants
who’s lifestyle involves preparing ingredients and cooking at home, contrasts
with perhaps what is more typical of a young person’s lifestyle in London, in
which restaurants and specialist food shops are accessible and affordable, and
home cooking is either for convenience or pleasure. And finally, practicality
29
© 2026 steflai.github.io - All Rights Reserved.
which is seen as a characteristic of Chinese-ness that my participants appeared
to take pride in.
Other interviewees such as Elise, Kitty and Holly agreed that there was an
emotional element to their liking and occasional craving for Chinese food, in fact
they were a bit surprised to hear that others had quite vehemently rejected
suggestions of emotion. Their replies to whether they missed Chinese food were
quite matter of fact: of course, everyone does. However this still seems to be less
intense and evocative than the Greek’s emotional attachment to certain foods
such as the ‘breast of Aphrodite’ peach described so emotionally by Seremetakis
(1994, p. 1).
Overall, it was unsurprising to find that the participants that felt more of
an emotional attachment were more willing to invest themselves in cooking and
recreating dishes in their own kitchens; especially since the process is quite
involving in terms of time, skill and effort. Going through the embodied process
of food preparation and cooking also means one becomes closely acquainted
with the ingredients and methods, leading to a more involved mode of
consumption that lends insight into the construction of an identity (Vannini et al,
2012, p. 112).
1.2 Recipes from the Internet (and some imagination)
The title of this section comes from a story Yan shared at the dinner party,
which everyone else found quite amusing and a bit outlandish: ‘I made fried rice
this afternoon, and I had [a bag of mixed salad] so a chopped up a bit for the
rice … I am imagining it to be like salt fish and chicken fried rice which has
shredded lettuce, so I added that imagination to my dish.’
30
© 2026 steflai.github.io - All Rights Reserved.
Unlike Greek food practices and techniques that are passed on through
generations (Sutton 2001, p. 126), which are mostly through the maternal line;
cooking amongst young Hong Kong Chinese is mostly self-taught from Internet
recipes, books and sharing among friends. During dinner with Holly, she
mentioned that sometimes she would miss her mother’s cooking, however when
she cooked herself, it was following recipes from books or the web.
The lack of a cooking tradition in Hong Kong could be because of a variety
of factors, some of these are: living space in Hong Kong is limited and as a result
kitchens are often very small, to the extent that can really only accommodate one
person so teaching and sharing techniques is understandably difficult. Eating out
is quite cheap, so much so that some couples never cook at home, and are known
as ‘riceless’ couples
1
. Many households employ domestic helpers who do the
cooking, therefore these youngsters would have grown up in a household where
mothers do not cook, and cooking would be seen as a mundane chore.
It is for these reasons that the meaning of ‘home cooking’ to a young
migrant from Hong Kong is much more diverse than what generally might be
assumed to be a mother’s or grandmother’s cooking; it may include take-out that
is often had at home during the family meal, or cooking by a domestic helper.
This combined with seeking recipes from the Internet, and sharing experiences
and techniques among friends by young migrants cooking to recreate Chinese
food means that there is much less linearity in the pathways of foods and dishes
from home to the migrant destination.
Somewhere along these rather loose and divergent pathways, a broader
understanding of ‘home foods’ seems to have arisen. Kitty says that while she

enjoys spicy and sour flavours, and cold and pickled dishes of cuisines more
typical of central and northern China, her mother eats very plainly, mostly rice
and steamed dishes. Therefore it is only through living on her own in London
that she has come to know foods that are of home, but not necessarily from her
own home.
The practices of cooking from recipes online, and learning from and
sharing with friends in London means that Hong Kong Chinese migrants are
drawing from a pool of knowledge which represents a collective identity and
taste. Outside elements such as what is trendy at the moment can more easily
enter into what might be visualized as a body of water fed by many streams,
compared to the single stream of family recipes passed down through
generations.
Robert and Keith have described to me quite practical approaches to food,
and it is in these that other ideas seem to be readily adopted. When cooking for
himself Robert aims for a balance of carbohydrates, vegetables and protein and
doesn’t mind repeating meals as long as he feels he is getting the necessary
nutrition. Keith in particular has incorporated Western notions of healthy eating
into his diet of what he identifies as Chinese food. He describes a typical meal as
rice, salmon and some salad and seeds, based on the idea of rice as a healthy
grain and fish as a lean protein. For seasoning he has vinaigrette dressing and
soy sauce, the latter which he says perhaps is unhealthy but he doesn’t care.
This example begs the question of what is Chinese food, or whether it can
be confined to a category or even be characterized by certain features. Through
observing and cooking with my participants, I noticed that the dishes they
cooked could be divided roughly into two categories: those that have a name, or
32
© 2026 steflai.github.io - All Rights Reserved.
require a specific recipe, and those that do not. Elise seems to prefer to make
dishes in the former category, and her cooking tends to have richer sauces and
more complex flavours, and somewhat resemble restaurant dishes. Whereas
Claire cooks making it up as she goes along, with stir-frying as a staple technique
and soy sauce, chicken powder and cooking wine as staple seasonings. The
resulting dishes would be plainer, which is less typically found in restaurants
and takeaways.
This spectrum of food identifiable as Chinese or with Chinese
characteristics that is regularly prepared and eaten by my participants shows
that there is great elasticity and ongoing change in not only the definition of
Chinese food as a category, but also the rules that govern preparation and
techniques. Can this be seen as an enactment of cosmopolitan identity? In my
introduction I chose a definition of cosmopolitanism that is fluid and constantly
being remade, which shows the connections between the local and the global
(Jones et al, 2014). I think as illustrated in this section, it can be seen that the
combination of being grounded and comfortable in one’s home cuisine, and also
incorporating elements from one’s immediate surroundings such as convenient
ingredients from the supermarket, or healthy eating advice. This also echo’s
Gruenberg’s (2014) exploration of definitions of nostalgia as something that
provides a stable base for ventures into the unfamiliar new world; a definition
which she still finds somewhat restrictive, so she finally settles on defining
nostalgic practices as performances of identity that allow new modes of
belonging.
However in the conversations captured during fieldwork, there is also a
significant amount of discussions about the characteristics, quality and

ultimately the authenticity of Chinese food, which I will consider more closely in
this next section.
‘
食
Chinese’
After dinner when we were in the kitchen making dessert, Elise asked me
why I thought when we talked about eating Chinese food, we would say ‘食 (sik)
Chinese’ saying the word ‘Chinese’ in English. I said maybe we were thinking of it
as a specific activity, that perhaps needed special preparations or specific
locations or restaurants; or perhaps we are subconsciously thinking that having
Chinese in London is not the authentic experience; or maybe we are simply
separating the experience from the more pedestrian one of having Chinese food
at home in Hong Kong. The question was left open.
The possible implication of inauthenticness is interesting, especially in
contrast to the ‘anything goes’ attitude described in the previous sections.
However it is important to remember that both a consciousness of authenticity
and perhaps thereby quality co-exists with the inventive free-spiritedness, and
the two are not contradictory.
I have gotten an interesting range of reactions when asking participants
how they feel about ‘fake’ Chinese food:
‘A spring roll, even if it just has some shredded carrot and minced pork
inside, if it is crispy and fresh and has something savoury inside you will still
find it good to eat. Even if you know it is a different standard to Hong Kong.
It is obvious, but you don’t find it offensive, but actually grateful that it is
there for you’. – Kitty
‘I think anything with Chinese sausage can be made with bacon.’ – Paul
34
© 2026 steflai.github.io - All Rights Reserved.
Others such as Wilson and Ernest reacted quite strongly that ‘fake’ or
Anglicised Chinese food was a definite no. Their reactions seemed encompass a
mild disgust combined with a sense of superiority in knowing what ‘real’ Chinese
food is.
What then can we make of Chinese foods unique to overseas Chinese,
such as prawn toast in the UK and fortune cookies in America? The negative
reactions to these sorts of foods were less strong, perhaps because these foods
are not so much bastardisations as new inventions that are unique to the local
landscape.
Keith’s response to the question about ‘fake’ Chinese food is an extreme
example that shows how impossible it can be to come to a consensus on what is
authentic. Born and bred in North London, Keith says: ‘For me, [London Chinese
food] is the real stuff. When I went to Hong Kong and I had it. I was like, what’s
going on, why’s the food so bland… You see, my set of norms, real Chinese food, is
Shaftsbury Avenue basically. When I go to Kowloon or something its like, ehh,
what is this? I think my tastes are a bit twisted. My idea of what is Chinese is
London.’
In other cases, authenticity is not always desired. Robert says he thinks
China town is a caricature of Chinese restaurants, particularly in the light of a
recent Guardian article ‘Goodbye to the rudest restaurant in London – Wong Kei
is finally ditching the bad attitude’ (Williams, 2014). He says he thinks
restaurants rely on the entertainment value of having ‘authentically’ rude staff
and shabby décor and therefore avoid modernising and improving, but he
35
© 2026 steflai.github.io - All Rights Reserved.
personally would much prefer trendy places like Plum Valley, ‘where you can
actually have a date’.
Claire also tells an interesting story of an instance where authenticity is
an unwanted quality: ‘We went to a Chinese restaurant in Shropshire once,
because after a few days of pub food I was feeling a bit sick of it… and the lady
behind the counter said “no, that menu is for gwailo (Westerners)”. The one we
were looking at above the counter had dishes like chicken with vegetables and
beef with mushrooms. “this one”, she said, taking out another menu “is for
Chinese. It has stuff like 麻婆豆腐 (maa pod dau fu, spicy tofu）. But I didn’t get
why there must be a strict division that Chinese must want ‘Chinese’ food. And
the gwailo food was cheaper!’
After looking at these various examples, what does authenticity say about
the identities constructed around it? And how important is authenticity?
Referring back to my introductory chapter, authenticity is not an objective
measure, however knowledge and claims of authenticity are used to bolster
one’s social and cultural standing. In the case of the migrant, authenticity maybe
more about personal enjoyment than social status, such as in cases of finding a
flavour or smell that so closely resembles that of home.
Authenticity is closely linked with cosmopolitanism, as it is both a feature
and measure of it. However, this somewhat Eurocentric view actually also is
applicable to Hong Kong Chinese in Hong Kong, so it might actually be ‘native-
centric’ rather than simply ‘Western’. In London, if cosmopolitanism is the more
fluid concept of connections between the global and the local, the distant and
specific (Jones et al, 2014), then perhaps the letting go of the strict rules of
36
© 2026 steflai.github.io - All Rights Reserved.
authenticity can be seen as a mark of a cosmopolitan identity. This is because it is
a sign of not clinging tightly to ‘how things were at home’, but being able to
change and adapt to create a sense of home and belonging in a new place while
fitting into a new society.
In the case of Hong Kong Chinese migrants, experience and knowledge of
authenticity is a given, and therefore may be treated as lightly or seriously as one
pleases. When amongst friends of other ethnicities, the migrant becomes the
expert on the authenticity of that cuisine and can play at being the embodiment
of the exotic and the ultimate cosmopolitan. While I doubt many would take this
facet of their migrant identity seriously, it is interesting to consider how the
migrant shapes or constructs his or her identity in different circles of migrant life
as we move on to the next chapter ‘home’.
